query: What missing‑data rules, imputation predictors, and exclusion thresholds (physio channel failure, low scale ICC, excessive motion) should be preregistered to avoid post hoc subject removal?

response.query: What missing‑data rules, imputation predictors, and exclusion thresholds (physio channel failure, low scale ICC, excessive motion) should be preregistered to avoid post hoc subject removal?
response.answer: Preregister rules for missing data: use multiple imputation, exclude predictors with >30% missingness, set low intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) threshold, and exclude subjects with excessive motion.

What kinds of metrics can I use to make the decision between removal of the predictor, listwise removal, imputation or some other options? How should I deal with a predictor with 20% - 25% missing when I have reason to believe that it's MNAR? I'm thinking of using imputation on the remaining predictors with around 5% missingness. One of the advantages of multiple imputation instead of a single imputation of missing data is that the result incorporates the variability introduced by the imputation process while in principle using all the available information. It might be worse to omit such a variable, as information in the cases having values for that variable might improve the imputations for other variables. Even if for some reason you don't keep it as a predictor variable, it can still be included as part of the imputation process. The link above provides a simple introduction to the process of generating and using the multiple sets of imputations. With this number of predictors it might be best to do the imputations first and then do feature selection if feature selection is really necessary. The chained-equation approach makes it straightforward to deal with imputations of several variables at a time. First, if one of your predictors is really "missing not at random" (MNAR) in the technical sense, then you will need to use special care and develop a joint model of the outcome variable and the predictor. If there are some predictors that are likely to be missing in many cases going forward, not just frequently omitted from your present data set, and you are going to be making predictions on a case-by-case basis, then you have to consider carefully how you would make your predictions in such cases and whether that variable should be included in your model. Bring the best of human thought and AI automation together at your work. # Multiple imputation with some missing baseline data and with some missing longitudinal data. How shall I impute the data in the following situation: I have some baseline covariates collected and longitudinal data. Both baseline covariates and longitudinal data have some missing data. Shall I impute first baseline covariates using regression imputation of the missing baseline covariates based on all other variables. And then when baseline covariates are imputed, use multiple imputations for longitudinal outcome? ## 1 Answer 1. In general, you should impute all those missing values, both predictors and outcomes, together. Stef van Buuren shows how in Flexible Imputation of Missing Data. He quotes Donal Rubin at the beginning of Chapter 2 to explain why that's important:. Imputing one value for a missing datum cannot be correct in general, because we don’t know what value to impute with certainty (if we did, it wouldn’t be missing). That said, in some circumstances it might be good enough to use single imputation. See Chapter 3 of Frank Harrell's Regression Modeling Strategies, with a summary in Section 3.11. It also might not be necessary to impute the missing outcome observations at all, depending on how you are modeling time with your longitudinal data. With a flexible model of time it might be possible to use the data you have and not worry about having some missing time points for some individuals. See Chapter 7 of the Harrell reference. results.content: # Missing Data Imputation Approaches | How to handle missing values in Python. Missing values in data degrade the quality.**. One of the common problems with real raw data is, they often contain missing values. ## Types of missing values. ## What to do when the data is missing? When there are missing values in data, you have four options:. * **Approach 1:** Drop the row that has missing values. * **Approach 3:** Impute the missing data, that is, fill in the missing values with appropriate values. * **Approach 4:** Use an ML algorithm that handles missing values on its own, internally. **Question: When to drop missing data vs when to impute them?**. An exception of course is when you KNOW for certain what the data should be if the values are missing. *For example, if the data is about exam scores which contains missing values, because the candidates didn’t give the exams. You can visualize missing values in the data using `missingno` package. ## Do the missingness of values in one column affect the missing data behaviour in another? ## How to impute missing values? When imputing with missing values, broadly you have two approaches. * Mean of entire column excluding the missing values. * Mean or median of only those rows (of the variable) that has the same value of Y as the missing. 2. **Predict the missing value with machine learning** using other non-missing columns as predictors. ## **Approach 1: Dropping rows that contail missing values**. **Depending on the context you can fill missing data with a standard, meaningful value.**. 6. **Predicting the missing values**. Fill missing values with the most frequent values. * **If the data were missing completely at random**, then mean /median imputation might be suitable. Therefore, replacing missing values by the mean and the median are almost equivalent. Having said that, you should avoid filling with mean, if you observe and increasing or decreasing trend in your data, in which case you might want to consider ‘interpolation’ and [predicting the missing value using ML approach]. Interpolation is another useful strategy to impute missing values. **[Next] Lesson 7:** MICE imputation – How to predict missing values using machine learning in Python.
